title: all, every, whole
subtitle: all day / every day / the whole day
summary: Learn when to use everybody/everything rather than all, when to use whole instead of all, and the difference between every day, all day and all the time.

lesson.heading: everybody / everything, not all
lesson.text: We do not normally use **all** on its own to mean *everybody* or *everything*. We say **everybody / everyone** for people and **everything** for things.

examples.text: Our holiday was a disaster. **Everything** went wrong.

lesson.heading: How we use all
rows: **All** I've eaten today is a banana.

lesson.heading: whole = complete, entire
lesson.text: **Whole** means *complete* or *entire*. We use it mostly with singular countable nouns, and we put **the / my / a** etc. before it.

examples.note: = all the book, not just a part of it

examples.text: Emily has lived **her whole life** in the same town.
I was so hungry, I ate **a whole packet** of biscuits.

lesson.heading: not whole with uncountable nouns
lesson.text: We do not normally use **whole** with uncountable nouns such as *water, food, money, information, luggage*. We use **all** instead.

examples.text: Did you spend **all the money** I gave you?
When I was on holiday, **all my luggage** was stolen.

lesson.heading: every day / all day
lesson.text: We use **every** to say how often something happens. **All day** or **the whole day** means the complete day from beginning to end.

examples.text: When we were on holiday, we went to the beach **every day**.
The bus service is excellent. There's a bus **every ten minutes**.
We spent **all day** on the beach. or We spent **the whole day** ...
Dan was very quiet. He didn't say a word **all evening**.

lesson.heading: all the time or every time?

left.label: all the time
examples: They never go out. They are at home **all the time**.
I don't like the weather here. It rains **all the time**.

right.label: every time
examples: **Every time** I see you, you look different.
It's a very sad song. **Every time** I hear it, it makes me cry.

lesson.heading: A singular verb, but they/their
lesson.text: **Every / everybody / everyone / everything** are singular words, so the verb after them is singular. But we use **they / them / their** to refer back to *everybody* and *everyone*.

examples.text: Every seat in the theatre **was** taken.

lesson.text: Count the noun: a whole packet, a whole day (countable) but all the money, all my luggage (uncountable).

exercises.prompt: It was a good party. ___ had a great time.
exercises.explanation: We do not use all on its own for people: everybody (or everyone) had a great time.

exercises.prompt: Nothing has changed. ___ is the same as it was.
exercises.explanation: For things we say everything, not all.

exercises.prompt: I'm really exhausted. ___ I want to do is sleep.
exercises.explanation: All I want to do = the only thing I want to do.

exercises.statement: Everybody have arrived, so we can start the meeting.
exercises.explanation: Everybody has arrived, so we can start the meeting. Everybody takes a singular verb.

exercises.prompt: I read the book from beginning to end. I read ___.
exercises.explanation: The whole book = all the book, not just a part of it.

exercises.prompt: Everyone in the team played well. Say the same thing using whole.
exercises.explanation: We put the before whole: the whole team = the complete team.

exercises.prompt: Paul opened a box of chocolates and didn't stop until there were none left. He ate ___.
exercises.explanation: Whole = complete, and box is a singular countable noun.

exercises.prompt: The bus service is very good. There's a bus ___.
exercises.explanation: We use every to say how often something happens.

exercises.prompt: I'm tired. I've been working hard ___.
exercises.explanation: We say all day (not all the day) for the complete day from beginning to end.
Correct. Everybody takes a singular verb, but we use they/themselves afterwards.

exercises.prompt: It's a very sad song. ___ I hear it, it makes me cry.
exercises.explanation: Every time = each time, on every occasion. All the time means always, continuously.

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence need whole or all in the gap (shown as ...)?

items.text: Did you spend ... the money I gave you?
Emily has lived her ... life in the same town.
I was so hungry, I ate a ... packet of biscuits.
When I was on holiday, ... my luggage was stolen.
It was a terrible fire. The ... building was destroyed.
